prompt: Should schools require uniforms
text:
I think schools should require uniforms because it makes things more fair for everyone. Right now kids compare clothes all the time and people who cant afford brand name stuff feel bad about it. My friend Marcus got teased for his shoes last year and he stopped coming to lunch for a week. If everyone wears the same thing that problem mostly goes away.

Also uniforms save time in the morning. You dont have to think about what to wear or fight with your mom about outfits. Parents spend less money too since you only need a few shirts and pants instead of a whole closet. My cousin's school has uniforms and she said she likes it because she just grabs the same thing every day.

Some people say uniforms take away freedom to express yourself. I get that, but school is not really a place for fashion shows. You can still show who you are through clubs, sports, art, and how you act. Plus the uniform can be like a team thing that makes the school feel more united.

I know some students hate the idea and think it looks boring. But I think the benefits are bigger. Fairness, less stress in the morning, and less money spent is a good combination. So yeah, I think schools should require them.

prompt: Should schools require uniforms
text:

First reason is equality. With uniform, nobody can show their money or social status through clothes. Students focus more on study and friendship instead of comparing. In my school in Seoul, we never worry about what we wear, so we talk about more important things.

Second reason is convenience. In the morning, student does not need to choose clothes. This save time and reduce stress. Parents also benefit because they do not need to buy many clothes every season. Uniform is usually more cheap than normal fashion clothes.

Some people think uniform limit creativity and individual expression. I understand this argument. However, students can express themselves in other ways, such as art class, music, sports, and club activities. School is for learning, so clothes is less important than it.

In conclusion, I believe school should require uniform. It makes students more equal, saves time and money, and help create school spirit. Therefore, I think uniform policy is good for students.

prompt: Should schools require uniforms
text:
Nowadays, many schools in the world are discussing about uniforms. I believe that schools should require uniforms for students. In my country, Iran, students wear uniform in schools from primary to high school. Everybody wears same color and style, so there is not much difference between rich and poor students.

One important reason is that uniform make students more equal. When students wear different expensive clothes, some students feel sad because they cannot buy them. A uniform solve this problem. Also, teachers can focus on lessons and not on the fashion of students.

Another reason is that uniforms save money. Families spend a lot of money every year for buying new clothes for school. With uniform, they only need two or three sets. It is more economic for family, especially for families with many children.

Some people say uniform is boring and it limits freedom. This is true that students cannot wear what they like. But school has rules for behaviour and it is normal. Students can express their personality in their hobbies, their art and their friendship.

For these reasons, I think schools should require uniforms. It helps students to be equal, save money and focus on study. In my opinion, uniform is a good idea for all schools.

prompt: Should schools require uniforms
text:
School uniforms are a topic that comes up every few years, and I think the case for them is stronger than many people admit. The most important argument is equality. When every student wears the same clothes, students cannot be judged by the brands they wear or the money their families have. This matters most for younger students, who often feel pressure to keep up with classmates.

Uniforms also make mornings simpler. Students don't have to spend twenty minutes deciding what to wear, and parents don't have to argue about outfits that are too short or too loud. Over a school year, families often save a lot of money, because a uniform costs less than a wardrobe built around current trends.

Critics argue that uniforms limit self-expression. That concern is real, and students should have room to show who they are. Still, school already has many rules about behavior, and self-expression can happen through clubs, art, music, sports, and the way students treat each other. A uniform does not erase personality. It just moves the focus away from clothes.

Finally, uniforms can build a sense of community. Wearing the same thing creates a shared identity, which is useful at schools where students come from very different backgrounds. For these reasons, I believe schools should require uniforms, while still allowing reasonable exceptions for religious and medical needs.

prompt: Should schools require uniforms
text:
I used to hate uniforms. In seventh grade I had to wear a polo and khakis every day, and I thought it was the most boring thing ever. My little sister went to a school with no uniform and she always looked like she was having more fun. But after a few years I changed my mind a bit, mostly because of what happened with my neighbor's kid.

Here is the thing. Kids notice clothes. They notice who has the new sneakers and who wears the same jacket for three winters. Uniforms take that away, at least during school hours. Nobody can say you're poor because your shirt is from a discount store, because everyone's shirt is the same. I think that matters more than people give it credit for.

Mornings are also way less chaotic. My mom used to do a whole thing every Sunday night, laying out outfits, and then on Monday somebody would hate their outfit and cry. A uniform fixes that. You grab the shirt and you go.

I know the argument about self-expression is real. My sister would probably still complain about it. Kids should get to show who they are. But honestly you can do that with the stuff you pick for clubs, or the way you draw, or the music you listen to. Not everything has to be about what you wear on a Tuesday.

I don't know, maybe uniforms are not the answer to everything. Schools have bigger problems. But if it helps some kid feel less judged, I think it's worth it. I guess I'd say schools should require them, although I'm still a little bit torn about it, if I'm being honest.

prompt: Are video games good for learning
text:
Video games get a bad reputation, but I think they can actually be good for learning. My little brother plays a game about building cities and he knows way more about money and resources than I did at his age. He doesnt even realize hes learning, which is kind of the point.

Some games make you think ahead. You have to plan, figure out what happens if you do one thing, and then fix your mistakes. That is basically problem solving. In strategy games you learn about history too, like how empires worked or why certain battles happened. My history teacher even said some students knew more about the Roman army because of a game.

Games also help with teamwork and communication. When you play with friends online you have to coordinate, talk fast, and figure out roles. Some games have reading and vocabulary that is hard, and kids learn new words without a dictionary.

Of course games can be bad if you play too much or only play violent stuff. Parents should set limits. But the idea that all games are a waste of time is not true. If a game is picked carefully, it can teach you a lot. So I think video games can be good for learning, as long as you dont overdo it.

prompt: Are video games good for learning
text:
Video games are often seen as a waste of time, but I think they can be useful for learning. When I was young in Korea, my parents thought games were bad. However, I learned a lot from some games. For example, I played a game about building cities, and I learned how to manage money and resources. This is similar to economics.

First, many games need problem solving. Player must think about the situation, make a plan, and try again when it fails. This skill is very important in school and also in real life. Second, some games have English text. When I was learning English, I played an adventure game and I had to read the story to continue. Because of this, my reading and vocabulary got better.

Third, online games teach teamwork. In a team game, players must communicate quickly and share roles. This is good practice for group projects at school. Also, some students learn history from strategy games because the games are set in historical times.

However, games also have problems. If students play too much, they lose sleep and study time. Some games contain violence that is not good for children. So parents and students need to choose games carefully and set limits.

In conclusion, video games can help people learn when they are used in the right way. I believe they are not only entertainment but also a tool for learning.

prompt: Are video games good for learning
text:
Many people think video games are only for fun and they are bad for students. But I believe video games can be good for learning if we choose them carefully. In my opinion, games have some benefits that are very useful for students.

The first benefit is that games improve problem solving. In many games, player must find a solution to difficult situations. For example, in puzzle games, you must think about the steps before you act. This way of thinking is similar to thinking in mathematics and science. My cousin is very good at logic because he plays these games every day.

The second benefit is language learning. Many games are in English, so players read instructions and dialogues. When I was learning English, I played a fantasy game and I learned many new words. It was more interesting than to study from a book only.

The third benefit is that some games teach history and geography. Strategy games show different countries and old civilizations. Students can learn about them in a fun way.

On the other hand, games can make students addicted and they can waste time. Violent games may also have bad effect on children. Therefore, parents must control the time and the content of games.

To conclude, video games can be good tools for learning when they are used in a balanced way. I think schools and parents should consider them as a useful resource.

prompt: Are video games good for learning
text:
Video games are usually dismissed as a distraction, but there is a good argument that they can support real learning. The strongest case is in problem solving. Many games require players to form hypotheses, test them, and adjust their strategy after failure. That cycle closely resembles the scientific method, and players practice it without being told to.

Games also expose students to language and information they might not encounter otherwise. Players read dialogue, follow complex instructions, and pick up vocabulary to understand a story. Strategy and simulation games can introduce history, economics, and geography in a context that feels relevant to students.

Multiplayer games build collaboration skills as well. Teammates must communicate under pressure, divide roles, and adapt when plans fail. These are the same skills that group projects demand, though in a much more immediate setting.

These benefits do not come automatically. Excessive play can displace sleep and homework, and some content is inappropriate for young players. Educators and parents should choose titles deliberately and set clear limits. Used thoughtfully, though, video games can be a legitimate tool for learning rather than only an entertainment problem to be managed.

prompt: Are video games good for learning
text:
Okay so I'll admit I'm biased. I spent a lot of my childhood on a computer playing a building game, and my parents yelled at me constantly. Now that I'm in college, I'm not sure they were completely right. I learned how to budget in that game before I ever learned it in a class, and I still remember the lesson about supply and demand.

The strongest argument, I think, is about trying things and failing. In a lot of games you die, you lose, you start over. That is annoying, but it also teaches you that failing is part of getting better. I wish more school felt like that. Grades make failure feel like a disaster.

Games also get weird with language. My friend learned most of his English from fantasy games, which is funny because he can say 'dragon' a hundred ways but still struggles with ordering food. Still, he reads faster than anyone I know.

Here's where I get worried. A lot of people, including me sometimes, lose way too many hours and skip sleep. Some games are honestly garbage and not something a kid should be playing. So I don't think every game is educational, and I don't think parents should just hand over a controller and walk away.

I guess my answer is yes, sometimes, depending on the game and how much you play. It's not a magic fix for school. But I wouldn't call it a waste of time either, which is what my dad still says every Thanksgiving.

prompt: Should the voting age be 16
text:
I think the voting age should be lowered to 16 because teenagers deal with a lot of the same things adults do. At 16 you can work, pay taxes in some places, and drive in many states. If you can do all that, it seems weird that you cant pick who makes the laws that affect you.

Lots of laws affect teens directly. School funding, public transportation, and even the minimum wage are things teenagers care about. We are the ones sitting in the classrooms with broken chairs and old computers. Why shouldn't we have a say in who decides about that?

Some people say 16 year olds are too young and dont understand politics. But a lot of adults dont really understand politics either. People vote based on whatever they saw on TV or their parents' opinions. Teens are actually pretty informed because we get news on our phones all day. Civics classes also teach us how government works.

Another reason is that voting can become a habit. If you start voting at 16 while you are still in school, you are more likely to keep voting when you get older. Many people who dont vote in their twenties just never started.

I know some people worry that teens will just follow their parents. That might happen sometimes, but adults do it too. So I think 16 is a good age for voting, and it would make our voice matter more.

prompt: Should the voting age be 16
text:
I believe that the voting age should be lowered to 16. In many countries, young people can work and pay taxes at 16, so they should also have the right to vote. In Korea, the voting age is 19, and I think that is too late. When I was 17, I already read news about politics and I had opinions about education and the environment. But I could not vote.

First, young people are affected by government decisions. Education policy, minimum wage, and public transportation all influence teenagers directly. If students cannot vote, their needs are often ignored by politicians. Politicians usually care more about older voters because they vote more.

Second, teenagers are becoming more informed. Many students use the internet and social media to read news. Some schools also teach about government and democracy. So sixteen year olds can understand important issues.

Third, voting early can create a good habit. If young people vote for the first time at 16, they will probably continue to vote in the future. This can increase participation in the whole country.

Some people say sixteen year olds are emotional and easily influenced. However, many adults are also influenced by media and friends. Age does not always decide maturity.

In conclusion, I think sixteen is a good age for voting. Young people deserve a voice in decisions that will shape their future.

prompt: Should the voting age be 16
text:
In my opinion, the voting age should be 16 years old. Many people think that young people are not mature enough to vote, but I do not agree with this idea. At the age of 16, people can already work in some countries, pay taxes and get married with permission. So it is strange that they cannot choose their government.

The first reason is that decisions of government affect young people very much. For example, education budget, school programs and job opportunities are important for teenagers. If young people can vote, politicians must listen to their problems and needs.

The second reason is that teenagers are informed about politics. Today students have access to news through the internet. They discuss social problems at school and on social media. In some countries, civic education is taught in schools so students know about democracy.

The third reason is that starting to vote early makes people more responsible citizens. When someone votes for the first time, they understand that their choice is important. This experience can continue for the rest of their life.

Of course some people say teenagers can be influenced by their friends or parents. But adults can also be influenced by advertisement and media. So maturity is not only about age.

For these reasons, I think 16 is a suitable age for voting. It would give young people a real voice in their country.

prompt: Should the voting age be 16
text:
Lowering the voting age to 16 is a reform worth taking seriously. Sixteen-year-olds already hold jobs, pay certain taxes, and in many places can drive. If society trusts them with those responsibilities, it is hard to justify excluding them from electing the officials who write the laws that govern those same activities.

Policy decisions affect young people directly. School funding, public transit, and the minimum wage shape daily life for teenagers, yet they often have no electoral leverage over those issues. Politicians tend to focus on older voters, who turn out at higher rates, so the concerns of younger citizens can be easily overlooked.

Critics argue that sixteen-year-olds lack the maturity to vote wisely. However, judgment is not determined by age alone, and many adults vote based on habit, advertising, or the opinions of people around them. Teenagers also have unusually easy access to news and political debate, and many already discuss current events in school.

Early voting may also build lasting habits. Research on civic participation suggests that people who vote in their first elections are more likely to keep voting. Giving sixteen-year-olds the right to vote could help establish that pattern sooner.

For these reasons, sixteen is a reasonable voting age, and it would make democracy more representative of the people it serves.

prompt: Should the voting age be 16
text:
I turned seventeen last spring and I still can't vote, which feels ridiculous when I think about how much I already deal with. I have a part time job, I pay taxes on it, and I'm expected to know how the economy works. But when my town had a vote about the bus route I actually take to school, I just watched the results come in and had no say at all.

That's the main reason I think 16 is fair. The stuff politicians decide affects us way more than people admit. School funding decides whether we have working heaters. Transit decides whether I can get to my job. Adults talk about 'the future' like it is far away, but for us it's next year.

Some people say teenagers don't know enough. I don't really buy that. My friends argue about politics constantly, sometimes too loudly, and honestly they're better informed than some grown ups I've heard at the grocery store. Not everyone, obviously. Some of my friends think about nothing but their group chat.

I also think voting at 16 could just make it a normal thing, like getting your license. You'd do it while you still have a teacher down the hall to ask questions. I'm not sure that would fix everything, and I'm still figuring out what I believe about a lot of this. But I'd want the choice, and I think most people my age would too.

prompt: Is social media harmful for teens
text:
Social media is a big part of teenage life now, and I think it can be really harmful. Almost everyone I know has an Instagram or TikTok, and a lot of them check it first thing in the morning and last thing at night. When you spend that much time looking at other people's lives, it is easy to feel like yours is not good enough.

The biggest problem is comparison. People post their best photos, their vacations, and their perfect friend groups. Then you look at your own messy room and feel bad. My friend Sofia stopped going to the beach with us because she didn't like how she looked in pictures, and I think social media made that worse.

Social media also takes up time. I have seen people stay up until two in the morning scrolling and then they are tired in class. Sleep is really important for teenagers and social media eats into it.

Cyberbullying is another issue. Mean comments and group chats can follow you home from school. At school you can at least walk away, but on your phone the drama never stops.

I dont think social media is all bad. It helps people stay in touch, find communities, and learn things. But for teenagers, the risks are big enough that I think it can be harmful, especially if there are no limits.

prompt: Is social media harmful for teens
text:
Social media has become a major part of teenagers' lives. I think it is harmful for teens in many ways, although it also has some benefits. In Korea, many students use social media every day, and I see my friends checking their phones during class and even at dinner.

The first problem is that social media makes teenagers compare themselves with others. People usually post only happy moments, so teens feel that their life is less interesting or less beautiful. In Korea, appearance is very important, so many students feel pressure to look perfect. This can cause stress and low self-esteem.

The second problem is sleep. Many teenagers use their phones late at night. Because of this, they are tired in the morning and they cannot concentrate in class. Sleep is very important for growing bodies and brains, so this problem is serious.

The third problem is cyberbullying. Online comments can be cruel, and they can spread quickly. Victims may feel afraid to go to school, and it is difficult for them to escape because the bullying continues on their phone.

However, social media is not completely bad. It helps students communicate with friends and find information for homework. Some students also learn new skills from videos.

In conclusion, I think social media is harmful for teenagers if they use it too much without control. Parents, schools, and students should work together to use it in a healthy way.

prompt: Is social media harmful for teens
text:
Nowadays social media is very popular among teenagers. Many of them spend hours every day on Instagram, YouTube and other applications. In my opinion, social media can be harmful for teenagers, because it affects their mental health, their sleep and their relationships.

First, social media can cause depression and anxiety. Teenagers see pictures of other people who look beautiful and successful, and they start to think that their life is not good. They compare themselves all the time. This comparison can make them feel lonely and unhappy.

Second, social media affects sleep. Many teenagers use their phone in bed and they do not sleep enough. When they are tired, they cannot study well and they become irritable. Sleep is necessary for health and memory, so it is very important to protect it.

Third, there is the problem of cyberbullying. Some students write unkind things about others on the internet. The victims cannot escape from these messages even at home. This can be very painful for them.

On the other hand, social media has some advantages. Teenagers can communicate with friends who live far away and they can learn about many topics. But I think the disadvantages are more serious.

Therefore, I believe social media is harmful for teenagers when they use it without limits. Parents and schools should teach them how to use it wisely.

prompt: Is social media harmful for teens
text:
Social media has become central to adolescent life, and its effects deserve more scrutiny than they usually receive. Many teenagers use platforms for hours each day, often during times that should belong to sleep or family. Heavy use is associated with several concerns that are hard to ignore.

The most documented problem is social comparison. Platforms reward curated images, and teenagers measure themselves against highlights rather than ordinary days. This dynamic can intensify anxiety about appearance and reduce self-esteem, particularly for young people already struggling with identity.

Sleep is another casualty. Notifications and endless feeds make it difficult to stop scrolling at night, and insufficient sleep harms memory, mood, and academic performance. Many students report being tired in class without recognizing that their phones are the reason.

Cyberbullying adds a further layer of harm. Unlike bullying in person, online harassment can follow a student home and reach a wide audience quickly. Victims often find no clear place of refuge.

None of this means social media is worthless. It keeps students connected, provides support communities, and offers educational content. Still, the costs are substantial enough that teenagers, parents, and schools should treat unrestricted use as a genuine risk.

prompt: Is social media harmful for teens
text:
I deleted Instagram in the middle of junior year and I'm still not totally sure it was the right call. Here's what happened. I started feeling worse about myself every time I opened it, which sounds dramatic but it was true. I'd look at my friends at a party they didn't invite me to, or some girl from a different school with a perfect skin routine, and then I'd spend the whole evening feeling like I was doing life wrong.

I don't think social media is evil. I still talk to my cousins in another state through it, and when my grandma figured out how to send videos, that was honestly great. But the way it's designed makes it really hard to stop. I'd tell myself I was going to check it for five minutes and suddenly it was midnight.

My sleep got bad. I was tired all the time and I couldn't remember what I'd read in history class, which is embarrassing to admit. My mom kept saying 'just put the phone away,' which is easy for her to say.

Some people my age handle it fine. I know a kid who posts every day and seems happier than anyone. Maybe it depends on who you are. But for a lot of teens I think it does real harm, especially the comparing part.

I don't know if I'll go back. I miss some of the stuff. Anyway, that's where I'm at right now, which is kind of annoyingly unresolved, but I guess that's teenage life.

prompt: Should students grade their teachers
text:
I think students should be allowed to grade their teachers, at least in an anonymous way. Teachers grade us all the time, and nobody asks us what we think of their teaching. Students are the ones who sit in those classes every day, so we know a lot about what works and what doesnt.

Some teachers are amazing and explain things clearly. Others just read from the slides and get mad when you ask questions. If teachers got feedback from students, they could figure out what they need to change. Even good teachers can get better when they know what confuses people.

People say students are too young or they will just give bad grades because they are mad. That can happen, which is why it should be anonymous and the results should be averaged out. One bad review because someone got a C should not ruin a teacher. But if twenty people say the same thing, the school should probably pay attention.

Some schools already do surveys at the end of the year, but they are usually boring and nobody takes them seriously. If the process was better designed, it could really help. Teachers also get evaluated by principals, but principals only see a class for a short time.

Overall, I think students should be able to grade their teachers. It makes school fairer and it helps teachers improve.

prompt: Should students grade their teachers
text:
I think students should be able to evaluate their teachers. In Korea, students often give evaluations at the end of semester, but the results are not always used well. In my opinion, student feedback is very important because students are the people who learn from teachers every day.

First, students know how the class feels. They know if the lesson is too fast, if the homework is too much, or if the teacher explains clearly. Principals or supervisors usually visit a class only once or twice, so they cannot see the whole situation. Students see it every day.

Second, feedback can help teachers improve. When a teacher knows what students find difficult, he or she can change the method of teaching. This can be better for everyone in the school.

However, there are some problems. Some students may give unfair grades because they are angry about a bad mark. So the evaluation should be anonymous, and the school should look at the average results rather than one opinion. If many students say the same thing, it is more reliable.

In conclusion, I believe students should be allowed to grade their teachers. It can make education more fair and help teachers become better. Schools should use this feedback carefully and with respect.

prompt: Should students grade their teachers
text:
In my opinion, students should have the right to evaluate their teachers. Teachers evaluate students with tests and grades every year, so it is fair that students also give their opinion about teachers. Education is a process for both sides, and the students are the ones who experience the lessons.

The first reason is that students know the quality of teaching better than anyone. They can see if the teacher is prepared, if the explanation is clear, and if the teacher is respectful. Administrators come to the class only for a short time, so they cannot know everything about the teacher.

The second reason is that feedback helps teachers to improve. If many students say the lessons are too fast, the teacher can change the speed. Most of the teachers want to do a good job, and this information can help them.

Of course, there are some problems. Students may be angry because of bad marks and they may give unfair comments. For this reason, the evaluation must be anonymous and the results should be studied carefully. One negative opinion should not decide the future of a teacher.

In conclusion, I think students should be able to grade their teachers in a respectful and anonymous way. It can improve the quality of education for everyone.

prompt: Should students grade their teachers
text:
Students should have a formal way to evaluate their teachers, provided the process is anonymous and carefully designed. Teachers evaluate students constantly through tests, grades, and comments, yet students rarely have a meaningful opportunity to assess how instruction is working from their side of the desk.

Students experience a teacher's methods every day. They can tell whether lessons are clear, whether feedback is useful, and whether expectations are fair. Administrators, by contrast, typically observe a class for a short period, which can miss patterns that students notice over an entire term.

Honest feedback can also help teachers improve. When many students report that a concept is confusing or that a pace is too fast, an instructor can adjust. Good teachers often welcome that information because it shows them what is actually happening in the room.

There are real risks, however. Students may give unfair ratings out of frustration with a grade, and a few harsh comments should not define an educator's career. The solution is anonymity, averaged results, and a review process that looks at trends rather than individual outbursts.

With those safeguards, student evaluations can make schools fairer and more responsive. Teachers, after all, are also learners.

prompt: Should students grade their teachers
text:
This is going to sound biased, but I think students should grade their teachers. I had a chemistry teacher last year who was honestly one of the best people I've met, and I'd still say that she couldn't explain a titration to save her life. Nobody ever told her that. The school never asked. I only figured it out because I failed the midterm and I was talking to my friend about it, and she said the same thing.

So that's my main point. Teachers are evaluated by principals who sit in the back for twenty minutes and leave. Meanwhile we're in there for five periods a day, we know exactly what's clear and what isn't. Something has to get to them.

I know the problem is people being petty. I've definitely wanted to write something mean about a teacher who gave me a C. So it has to be anonymous, and it should be averaged or read in bulk, not one angry comment at a time. Honestly I'd want that protection too.

I'm not sure how a school would do it without making a mess. There would be a lot of stupid comments, and some teachers would probably cry. But I think the information would be useful, and I'd rather have it than not. Anyway, that's about where I landed. It's not a perfect solution, but none of them are.

prompt: Is homework necessary
text:
I dont think homework is totally necessary, but I dont think we should get rid of it either. It really depends on how much and what kind. Some homework helps you remember stuff, but a lot of it is just busywork that takes hours and doesnt teach you anything new.

Homework does help practice. If you learn math in class, you need to do problems at home to actually get it. Reading at home also helps you get better at reading. Practice is important for almost every subject, so some homework is definitely useful.

But a lot of teachers give too much. I know kids who get three hours of homework a night and then they have no time for sports, family, or sleep. That is not healthy. Some kids also dont have a quiet place to work or a parent who can help them, so the homework is harder for them. That makes it unfair.

I think a better way is to give smaller amounts that are actually useful, like a few problems or a short reading. Teachers could also check if students understood it instead of just giving a grade for finishing.

So my answer is that homework is useful but only in small doses. We need to make it count and not just pile it up.

prompt: Is homework necessary
text:
Homework is a topic that many students discuss, especially in Korea where students study very hard. In my opinion, homework is necessary, but the amount should be reasonable. Too much homework can be harmful for students.

First, homework helps students practice what they learn in class. In mathematics, for example, students need to solve many problems to understand the method. Without practice, they may forget the lesson quickly. Homework also helps students develop self-discipline because they must manage their time.

Second, homework allows teachers to know which students need help. If many students get the same question wrong, the teacher can explain it again in the next class.

However, in Korea many students have homework and private lessons every night. They do not sleep enough and they have no time for hobbies or family. This is not healthy. Some students also have no quiet place at home, so homework becomes very difficult.

Therefore, I think homework is necessary, but teachers should give a suitable amount. Homework should be meaningful and not only a way to fill time. In conclusion, homework can be useful when it is balanced with rest and other activities.

prompt: Is homework necessary
text:
Homework is one of the most common things that students have to do after school. Some people think homework is necessary for learning, but others think it is a burden. In my view, homework is necessary, but it should be balanced and useful.

The main reason is that homework helps students to review what they learned in class. For example, in math, students need to practice many exercises to understand the lesson. If they do not practice at home, they will forget the material quickly. Also, homework helps students to be responsible and to organize their time.

Another reason is that homework gives teachers information about the level of students. When teachers read the homework, they can see which topics are difficult for the class and they can explain them again.

On the other hand, too much homework is a problem. Some students have several hours of homework every day and they cannot relax or sleep well. This makes them stressed and tired. Also, students who do not have a quiet place or help at home are in a difficult situation.

So I believe homework is useful when it is not excessive. Teachers should give meaningful tasks and consider the life of students outside school.

prompt: Is homework necessary
text:
Homework remains a standard part of school, but its necessity depends heavily on how it is designed. Practice is the strongest argument in its favor. Mathematics, languages, and science all improve through repetition, and many students would not consolidate a lesson without working through problems at home.

Homework also builds independence. Managing deadlines and completing tasks without supervision are skills that carry into college and careers. Assignments can show teachers which concepts are unclear, allowing them to reteach material where it is needed.

The problem is volume. Some students arrive home to several hours of assigned work each night, leaving little room for sleep, exercise, or family time. Students without a quiet place to work or an adult who can help face a steeper challenge, which can widen existing gaps.

A better model would emphasize quality over quantity. Short, targeted assignments that reinforce recent lessons are more useful than long worksheets completed mainly to earn points. Teachers can also check understanding rather than simply rewarding completion.

Homework is necessary in a limited sense, but its benefits disappear when it becomes excessive. The goal should be meaningful practice, not a nightly quota.

prompt: Is homework necessary
text:
I'm going to be honest, I hated homework for most of my life, and I still don't think I'd have learned half of what I know without it. Those two things are both true for me, which is why this question is harder than people make it seem.

When I was in ninth grade I had a math teacher who gave us ten problems every night, and I hated every single one. But I got really good at algebra. By the time the test came I could do it without thinking, and I'm pretty sure those nightly problems are why. Practice is boring and it works anyway.

Then there's the other side. My little cousin gets two hours of homework in fourth grade, which I think is insane. He cries about it. His mom has to sit with him, and she works two jobs. That's not learning, that's just a fight every night. I don't think his teacher is a bad person, she's probably just following some policy.

So I think homework is necessary, but I'd cut the amount in half and make the teachers actually look at it. I'm not totally sure what the right number is. Maybe it's whatever keeps kids from hating it, which is a weird standard. I guess that's what I'd want for my cousin anyway.

prompt: Is it better to live in a city or village
text:
I think living in a village is better than living in a city, at least for most people. In a village you know your neighbors and everybody kind of looks out for each other. My grandma lives in a small town and when she goes to the store, somebody always asks about her hip. In a city, people dont even know the person in the next apartment.

Villages are also quieter and less stressful. There is no constant traffic or sirens all night. You can actually see the stars, and there are fields and forests to walk in. Kids can play outside without their parents worrying as much about cars and strangers.

Cities have more jobs and better schools in some places, and that is a big deal. You also get more options for food, shopping, and things to do. If you want to be a doctor or an artist, a city probably gives you more chances. Public transport is usually better too, so you dont need a car.

But villages can have problems. Jobs are fewer, internet can be slow, and there might be only one doctor for miles. Some young people leave because there is nothing for them to do.

Overall I think village life is nicer for families and older people, but cities are better for ambitious young people. It really depends what you want out of life.

prompt: Is it better to live in a city or village

prompt: Is it better to live in a city or village
text:
Choosing between city and village life depends largely on priorities, but for many people the village offers a better foundation for everyday well-being. Smaller communities tend to be more connected. Neighbors know each other, and people often look out for one another in ways that are rare in crowded cities.

Villages also offer a quieter, cleaner environment. Less traffic and noise reduce daily stress, and access to fields and forests makes outdoor life easy. Children can often play outside with more freedom, and older residents can enjoy a slower pace.

Cities, however, provide advantages that villages struggle to match. They offer more employment options, larger universities, specialized hospitals, and a wider range of cultural and social activities. Public transportation is usually more reliable, reducing the need for a car.

Villages can also suffer from limited internet access and fewer services. For people whose careers depend on specialized jobs or fast connectivity, these gaps can be serious.

For families and retirees, a village often provides a healthier and more stable life. For ambitious young professionals, a city may be the better launchpad. The right answer depends less on the place itself than on what a person needs at each stage of life.

prompt: Is it better to live in a city or village
text:
I grew up in a village of about nine hundred people and I left the second I could. For a long time I thought that was the right move, because the city was where things happened. Now I'm not so sure. I miss the weird stuff about home that I used to hate, like how the guy at the gas station knows what kind of coffee you drink.

The city gave me everything I thought I wanted. Good jobs, a bunch of museums, food from twenty different countries within a few blocks. I'm not going to pretend that isn't amazing. But I also spend about an hour a day in traffic and I barely know anyone on my floor. Last winter I got sick and nobody checked on me for three days, which scared me more than I'd like to admit.

My mom says the village is dying because all the young people leave. I think she's partly right, and that's sad. There's a lot of truth in the idea that small places need people to stay, and I feel kind of guilty about it.

So I don't think one is better in general. Maybe it's better for a certain stage of life. I'd probably go back someday when I'm older, when I want quiet and a garden. For now I'm glad I'm here, though I'd be lying if I said I never think about the quiet, or the stars I can't see from my apartment.

prompt: Should junk food be banned in schools
text:
Junk food should be restricted, and in most cases banned outright, from school grounds. Schools are responsible for both education and student well-being, and vending machines stocked with candy and soda work against the lessons teachers deliver in health class.

The health case is clear. Foods high in sugar, salt, and saturated fat contribute to obesity, dental problems, and long-term disease. Rates of childhood obesity have risen sharply in many countries, and schools reach nearly every child during the day.

prompt: Should junk food be banned in schools
text:
When I was in middle school the vending machine was the most popular place in the building. Everyone had a dollar and a plan. I was one of those kids.
